newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.S. energy chief raps Total oil talks with Iran.
newsitem.headline: U.S. energy chief raps Total oil talks with Iran.

text.p: The United States on Thursday criticised a $3.5 billion gas contract French oil firm Total hopes to sign with Iran, saying it hoped the deal would not be finalised.
U.S. Energy Secretary Federico Pena, visiting Paris for international oil consumer talks, said the U.S. administration was sticking to its position of discouraging dealings with Iran.

"We certainly are discouraging that and we hope that's not the case," Pena told Reuters, referring to the deal to develop the giant South Pars gas field, which Iran has declared Total is likely to win.

His remarks were the first such high-level U.S. response to the latest French oil negotiations with Iran, which fly in the face of U.S. attempts to punish non-U.S. investment in Iran and have been backed by the French foreign ministry.
Foreign ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said on Tuesday that negotiations between French companies and Iran were "entirely legal" and faced no international restrictions.

Iran's Foreign Affairs Minister Ali Akbar Velayati said on Sunday Tehran had already awarded the South Pars contract to Total, though Total afterwards denied this and said "advanced discussions" were still continuing.
Total's investment in South Pars, if confirmed, would be the largest single foreign investment in Iran since the country's Islamic revolution in 1979.
The United States has repeatedly warned its allies against developing commercial ties with Iran, which it regards as a sponsor of international terrorism.

Total signed a $600 million deal with Iran to develop its offshore Sirri E and A fields in May 1995 after the Clinton administration blocked a similar deal with a U.S. oil firm and banned virtually all U.S. trade and investment with Iran.
The United States also in 1996 passed legislation designed to stop non-U.S. companies from doing business with Iran, a move strongly contested by France and its European partners.
Pena said he did not consider U.S. sanctions on three of the world's leading oil suppliers -- Iraq, Libya and Iran -- as posing a threat to U.S. oil supplies. "Thus far not," he said.

Pena will be meeting French and other Western energy ministers at a gathering of the 24-nation International Energy Agency on Friday. But a source close to the talks said the dispute on Iran was not likely to be broached formally.
